balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Humana Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Humana Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Humana Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Humana Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Humana Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Humana Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Humana Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Humana Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Humana Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Humana Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

membership.title: Membership
membership.content:
Total membership is every member Humana insures across Medicare Advantage, Part D, Medicaid, military (TRICARE) and specialty products; Individual and Group MA are the two Medicare Advantage books that carry the highest premium per member and the most CMS Star Ratings risk.

For Humana Inc.: Individual MA is ~58% of revenue and the segment management is actively managing through 2027 plan-year exits from 3.5-star-or-below contracts (~600k members, ~8% of the MA base), with roughly 40% expected to be recaptured into other Humana plans rather than lost to competitors.

What to watch:

  • Individual MA growth slowing or reversing as low-rated contracts are deliberately shed
  • Group MA and specialty/military membership offsetting any MA softness
  • Commercial membership is blank from 2026 onward -- Humana exited that business

benefitRatio.title: Benefit ratio and operating cost ratio
benefitRatio.content:
The health benefits ratio (medical loss ratio) is medical claims paid as a percentage of premium revenue -- the single most important margin driver for a health insurer. The operating cost ratio is SG&A as a percentage of revenue, the overhead layer on top of it.

For Humana Inc.: FY2026 guidance is a benefit ratio "slightly above 94%", a reversal from FY2025's 90.2%, driven by the 2026 CMS Star Ratings bonus-payment headwind (contract H5216's fall to 3.5 stars); Q3 2026 ran favorably at 93.9% on moderating inpatient utilization, and management's 2028 target is at least 3% MA pretax margin as the much-improved 2027 Star Ratings (93-95% of members in 4-star-plus plans) flow into 2028 bonus payments.

What to watch:

  • Benefit ratio trending toward or away from the FY2026 guide
  • Quarter-to-quarter swings from utilization trend versus the multi-year Star Ratings bonus lag
  • Operating cost ratio creeping up would offset any benefit-ratio improvement

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue: Insurance vs CenterWell
segmentRevenue.content:
Humana reports two segments: Insurance (Medicare Advantage, Part D, Medicaid, military) which takes on medical risk, and CenterWell (pharmacy, primary care, home solutions) which delivers care and is intended to lower the medical costs the Insurance segment pays out.

For Humana Inc.: CenterWell's total segment revenue (shown here) includes a large intersegment component -- services sold to Humana's own Insurance segment -- so it overstates CenterWell's external scale; its revenue mix to outside customers is roughly a fifth of the total shown.

What to watch:

  • CenterWell growing faster than Insurance, consistent with the owned-care-delivery strategy
  • Intersegment CenterWell revenue as a vertical-integration signal, not pure external growth

segmentIncome.title: Segment operating income: Insurance vs CenterWell
segmentIncome.content:
Operating income by segment shows where Humana's profit is actually earned: the Insurance segment's spread between premiums and medical costs, versus CenterWell's margin on pharmacy, primary care and home services (including what it earns serving Humana's own members).

For Humana Inc.: Insurance segment income is the one most exposed to the 2026 Star Ratings bonus headwind and benefit-ratio swings; CenterWell's income is the steadier, less CMS-cycle-dependent half of the business.

What to watch:

  • CenterWell cushioning an Insurance segment downturn (or not)
  • Either segment turning negative, as Insurance briefly did in Q3 2026 on an operating-income basis

govPrograms.title: Medicare vs Medicaid segment revenue
govPrograms.content:
Medicare segment revenue is premiums from Medicare Advantage and Part D; Medicaid is premiums from state Medicaid and dual-eligible contracts. Both sit inside the Insurance segment but are managed and reimbursed under very different rules (CMS Star Ratings bonus cycle for Medicare; state rate-setting for Medicaid).

For Humana Inc.: Medicare is roughly 8x the size of Medicaid and is where the FY2026 benefit-ratio and Star Ratings story plays out; Medicaid/dual-eligible/military/specialty together are a smaller but growing ~13% of revenue.

What to watch:

  • Medicaid growth as a diversification away from Medicare's bonus-payment cyclicality
  • Either program's revenue decoupling from its membership trend (rate changes, risk-adjustment)
